body:
History

The chillum is one of the oldest pipe shapes still in everyday use, and its history is older than the bong, the spoon, and the vaporizer put together. It traces back to India, where Hindu holy men, sadhus, used conical clay chillums in religious and communal settings, with the earliest documented use in the eighteenth century and some researchers pushing the first evidence back to the eighth century. The shape spread to Africa and to Rastafarian communities, and it reached the West in the 1960s and 1970s, and the geometry barely changed along the way: a straight tube, wide at the bowl end, narrow at the mouthpiece, with no carb hole, no water chamber, and no moving parts. Over time the same basic form was copied, adapted, and refined by many makers, so the record today covers a family of closely related objects rather than a single patented shape. The sources cited at the end of this record give the reader places to check each stage, and the history matters because it explains why the parts are arranged the way they are: each feature survives because it solved a practical problem for the people who used the supply every day.

The supply in detail

The chillum works by being the simplest pipe there is: a straight tube, wider at the bowl end and narrower at the mouthpiece, with ground herb packed into the wide end and smoke drawn straight through. It is made from borosilicate glass, and a common example measures about 130 mm long, with a bowl end 22 mm across, a mouthpiece 10 mm across, and a chillum stone, a small fitted pebble or ceramic piece, set inside to stop loose material reaching the mouth. There is no carb hole, so the air path is one straight line, and the draw is direct and quick. The parts fit together in a fixed order, and each part has one job: to hold the material, to apply the mechanism, or to carry the result to the user. Because the parts are simple and the mechanism is mechanical rather than electronic in its basic form, the supply can be understood by inspection, measured with a ruler, and checked by the arithmetic in this record. A chillum is the oldest supply in this lane, and that age is the design, not an accident.

Parts and variants

Each part of this supply can be inspected on its own, and the variants in the specification show how the same working principle is kept while size, material, and finish change. A larger version holds more and works more slowly or more steadily; a smaller version is easier to carry and quicker to clean. Makers choose materials for the job each part does: a part that meets heat needs a material that tolerates heat, a part that meets water needs a material that does not rust or swell, and a part that is handled often needs a surface that stays grippy and does not crack. The scale variants at the end of this record carry that same logic further, showing the design at pocket, standard, and workshop sizes, so the reader can see which dimensions change with scale and which stay the same.

Spec

Materials: Signature glazed stoneware clay tube; chillum stone of fitted ceramic; safi cloth included

Dimensions: Tube 130 mm long; bowl end 22 mm across; mouthpiece 10 mm across; outer diameter 28 mm at the bowl end; stone 12 mm across

Mechanism: Ground herb packed in the wider Signature bowl end; flame lights the surface; smoke travels straight through the tapered bore to the mouthpiece; the ceramic stone stops loose material

Use: Set the stone inside, pack the bowl end by pressing and turning in ground herb, hold at a slight angle, light while drawing slowly, tap out the ash when spent

Care: Tap out ash after cooling; soak in isopropyl alcohol, rinse, and dry; handle ceramic carefully as it chips and cracks if dropped; keep the stone fitted or replace it if it loosens

Variants: Clay, glass, wood, stone, and metal; straight and slightly flared bores; with or without a safi cloth; pocket and ceremonial lengths

Materials and design

The chillum is a material-spanning design, and the choice is between clay, glass, wood, stone, and metal. Clay is the original material, chosen by the sadhus because it was everywhere, it tolerates heat, and it can be shaped by hand; clay is the Signature choice, chosen here because it is the original chillum material, it tolerates heat, and it can be shaped by hand.

Build it yourself

A clay chillum is a genuine studio build, and this record gives it in full, with one plain limit: it needs a kiln, so it is a pottery-studio build, not a home build. Start with a bag of cone 5 or cone 6 stoneware clay, the kind any pottery studio stocks, and wedge it until it is free of air pockets.

3D printing

The chillum itself is not 3D-printable in glass or clay on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives direct flame at the bowl end, so a printed chillum would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG chillum stand and stone holder.

Use and program

To use the chillum, set the chillum stone inside first, then pack the bowl end by pressing it gently into ground herb and turning it a quarter turn each way, until the bowl section is full but not compressed. Hold the chillum at a slight angle, bring the flame just over the edge of the bowl, and start a slow draw, then tap out the ash when the bowl is spent.

Science proof

A chillum works by direct flow, and its physics is the physics of a tapered tube. The bore is a frustum, a truncated cone, wider at the bowl end and narrower at the mouthpiece, so the smoke speeds up as the tube narrows, and the draw feels direct because nothing slows the air down: no water, no carb, no chamber. The chillum stone is the one clever part: a small fitted pebble set at the transition between the bowl and the passage, it acts as a screen that stops ash and ground fragments from reaching the mouth, and it forces the air against the tube walls, which cools the smoke more than a straight empty tube would. The traditional safi, a damp cloth wrapped around the mouthpiece end, cools the smoke further by evaporation, and cupped hands around the mouthpiece form a small chamber where smoke can collect and cool before it is inhaled. Fired stoneware clay matters because it tolerates the hot bowl end and the cool mouthpiece without cracking, and because clay is the original chillum material. The bore volume is the frustum formula, one third pi times length times the sum of the two end radii squared and their product, and the bowl section is a shorter frustum at the wide end. The numbers in the specification can be checked against this physics: measure the parts, apply the formulas in the math proof, and run the demo program, and the results should agree within the rounding the program reports.

Math proof

The demo treats the chillum bore as a frustum, a truncated cone. With a length of 130.0 mm, a bowl-end diameter of 22.0 mm, and a mouthpiece diameter of 10.0 mm, the radii are 11.0 and 5.0 mm, so the bore volume is one third pi times 130 times the sum of 121, 55, and 25, about 27,363 cubic millimetres, or 27.36 cubic centimetres. The chillum stone is a sphere 12.0 mm across, with a volume of about 905 cubic millimetres, so the free bore volume is about 26.46 cubic centimetres. The outer clay is a frustum from 28.0 mm to 16.0 mm across, about 50,650 cubic millimetres, leaving a clay volume of 23.28 cubic centimetres, and at a stoneware density of 2.4 grams per cubic centimetre the mass is 55.87 grams. The bowl section is the first 35.0 mm of the bore, where the diameter tapers from 22.0 to 18.77 mm, a volume of about 11.45 cubic centimetres, and at the stated packing density of 0.15 grams per cubic centimetre the herb capacity is 1.72 grams. Every number comes from the specification in this record, the formulas are shown in full, and the program prints each quantity so the reader can check the arithmetic. The computation runs twice with SHA-256 digests printed, so the reader can confirm it is deterministic.

Use and care

Set the stone inside, pack the bowl end by pressing and turning in ground herb, hold at a slight angle, light while drawing slowly, tap out the ash when spent Tap out ash after cooling; soak in isopropyl alcohol, rinse, and dry; handle ceramic carefully as it chips and cracks if dropped; keep the stone fitted or replace it if it loosens

Design study

This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. Its numbers come from its own design specification in this record, and its physics, arithmetic, and program can be checked from first principles.

Sources

This Signature design cites no public sources; its numbers come from its own design specification in this record.
build_yourself: A clay chillum is a genuine studio build, and this record gives it in full, with one plain limit: it needs a kiln, so it is a pottery-studio build, not a home build. Start with a bag of cone 5 or cone 6 stoneware clay, the kind any pottery studio stocks, and wedge it until it is free of air pockets. Roll the clay into a tapered tube on a flat board, 130 mm long, 22 mm across at the bowl end and 10 mm across at the mouthpiece, using a wooden dowel as a mandrel to keep the bore open: wrap the clay around the dowel, smooth the seam with a damp sponge, and slide the dowel out while the clay is still soft. Shape a small fitted chillum stone from the same clay, a 12 mm ball pressed flat on one side, and set it inside the bore at the transition between bowl and passage while the clay is leather-hard. Let the piece dry slowly under plastic until it is bone dry, which takes two or three days, then bisque fire it in the studio kiln to cone 04, and glaze fire it to cone 5 or 6 if a glaze is wanted, or leave it unglazed and burnished. Let the kiln cool completely before opening it, then check the bore with a pipe cleaner and the bowl capacity against the demo numbers before using it.

demo.code:
"""Demo: chillum bore frustum volume and bowl capacity — Signature Chillum."""
import hashlib, math
def compute():
    L = 130.0; d_bowl = 22.0; d_mouth = 10.0; od_bowl = 28.0; od_mouth = 16.0; stone_d = 12.0; bowl_len = 35.0; pack = 0.15; rho = 2.4
    R = d_bowl / 2.0; r = d_mouth / 2.0
    bore_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * L * (R ** 2 + R * r + r ** 2)
    bore_cm3 = bore_mm3 / 1000.0
    stone_mm3 = (4.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * (stone_d / 2.0) ** 3
    free_mm3 = bore_mm3 - stone_mm3
    free_cm3 = free_mm3 / 1000.0
    Ro = od_bowl / 2.0; ro = od_mouth / 2.0
    outer_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * L * (Ro ** 2 + Ro * ro + ro ** 2)
    clay_cm3 = (outer_mm3 - bore_mm3) / 1000.0
    mass_g = clay_cm3 * rho
    d_end = d_bowl - (d_bowl - d_mouth) * bowl_len / L
    bowl_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * bowl_len * (R ** 2 + R * (d_end / 2.0) + (d_end / 2.0) ** 2)
    bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
    capacity_g = bowl_cm3 * pack
    return {"bore_volume_mm3": round(bore_mm3, 2), "bore_volume_cm3": round(bore_cm3, 2), "stone_volume_mm3": round(stone_mm3, 2), "free_volume_cm3": round(free_cm3, 2), "clay_volume_cm3": round(clay_cm3, 2), "clay_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "herb_capacity_g": round(capacity_g, 2)}
def main():
    a = compute(); b = compute()
    sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
    for key in ['bore_volume_mm3', 'bore_volume_cm3', 'stone_volume_mm3', 'free_volume_cm3', 'clay_volume_cm3', 'clay_mass_g', 'bowl_volume_cm3', 'herb_capacity_g']:
        print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
    print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
    print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
    print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

description: The Signature Chillum is a Signature-made design study for chillum, a new design in the Signature Marijuana Supplies Database that reworks the familiar public form with one deliberate change. It keeps the job the same — ground herb packed in the wider Signature bowl end; flame lights the surface; smoke travels straight through the tapered bore to the mouthpiece; the ceramic stone stops loose material — but changes how the parts are arranged, using signature glazed stoneware clay tube; chillum stone of fitted ceramic; safi cloth included. The design is sized at tube 130 mm long; bowl end 22 mm across; mouthpiece 10 mm across; outer diameter 28 mm at the bowl end; stone 12 mm across, which sets every number in this record, from the chillum bore frustum volume and bowl capacity in the demo to the scale variants at the end. This record is a design study, not a real manufactured product, and nothing here claims the design has been built, tested, or sold. What it does offer is a complete, checkable design: a full specification, the physics of how it would work, worked arithmetic tied to its own dimensions, a runnable program that computes those numbers, and three boundless scale variants. Readers can follow the design from first principles, repeat the arithmetic by hand, and run the program to check every number. The record also gives the materials and design, a build-it-yourself section, 3D-printing directions, and a use program, so the design can be judged as a whole, not only as a set of numbers. Like every Signature record, it sits beside its public twin in the same pair, so the reader can compare the public form with the Signature reworking side by side.

materials_design: The chillum is a material-spanning design, and the choice is between clay, glass, wood, stone, and metal. Wood is warm in the hand but burns and holds smell, stone is heavy and cool but hard to shape, and metal is tough but conducts heat straight to the mouth. The wall is about 3 mm thick in clay, which is the working compromise: thinner walls are lighter but break more easily, thicker walls survive drops better but narrow the bore. The chillum stone is a fitted pebble or ceramic piece, and its tolerance is the fit: it must sit snugly at the transition between bowl and passage without blocking the air. The bore tolerance is the taper itself: a bore that narrows too fast chokes the draw, while a bore that barely narrows at all gives the smoke no acceleration and no cooling. The finish is clear glass with coloured accents, or unglazed clay with a burnished surface, and the design varies by length, by material, and by whether a safi cloth is used, while the working principle stays the same.

method: The method in this record is to describe the supply from its parts, its dimensions, and its mechanism, and then to check those claims with arithmetic and a runnable program. First the parts are named and their materials given, so the reader knows what is metal, what is glass, and what is paper. Then the dimensions are stated in millimetres, grams, watts, or litres, so every later number has a source. Then the mechanism is explained step by step, in the order the user actually follows it, so the reader can picture the motion or the flow. The science proof explains the physics behind that mechanism, and the math proof works the arithmetic from the stated dimensions. Finally the demo program computes the same quantities from the same numbers, prints them with units, and runs twice with SHA-256 digests, so the reader can repeat the whole check on their own machine without trusting this record on faith.
print3d: The chillum itself is not 3D-printable in glass or clay on a home printer, and this record says so plainly: home printers extrude plastic filament, and no plastic survives direct flame at the bowl end, so a printed chillum would melt and give off fumes. What is printable is the accessory that goes with it: a PETG chillum stand and stone holder. Print it in PETG, which tolerates warm water and cleaning better than PLA, with a 0.4 mm nozzle, a 0.2 mm layer height, 20 percent gyroid infill, and 3 perimeters, giving a wall about 1.2 mm thick. Print the stand flat on its base with supports under the cradle curve only, at a nozzle temperature of 235 degrees C and a bed temperature of 80 degrees C, with the fan at 50 percent. Print time (estimate): about 1 hour for the stand at standard size. Post-processing is simple: remove the supports from the cradle, check the 28 mm pocket with calipers, and sand the rim lightly if it is sharp. Unmodeled factors: wall thickness, supports, nozzle settings, printer motion, and material-specific slicing all change the real print time and strength, so the estimate is not a validated print job; measure the printed pocket before trusting it with a real glass chillum.
problem: The problem this supply solves is practical and narrow: chillum needs to be prepared or used evenly, reliably, and with ordinary tools, without waste and without guesswork. Before a standard form existed, users improvised, and the result was uneven preparation, spilled material, and parts that wore out or broke. A good supply therefore has to do three things at once: hold the material securely, apply its mechanism evenly across the whole load, and survive repeated use without losing its shape or its edge. It also has to be easy to clean, because residue builds up and changes how it works, and easy to measure, because its dimensions set its capacity. This record states the problem in those terms so the specification, the science proof, and the mathematics can each be checked against it, and so a reader can judge whether the design in the record actually answers the problem it claims to solve.

"""Signature Chillum — full working program.

Computes the same quantities as the record demo, as a documented module with a class and a run() method.
Run: python3 program.py
"""
import hashlib
import math


class SupplyCalculator:
    """Calculator for Signature Chillum."""

    def compute(self):
        """Return the computed quantities as a dict."""
        L = 130.0; d_bowl = 22.0; d_mouth = 10.0; od_bowl = 28.0; od_mouth = 16.0; stone_d = 12.0; bowl_len = 35.0; pack = 0.15; rho = 2.4
        R = d_bowl / 2.0; r = d_mouth / 2.0
        bore_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * L * (R ** 2 + R * r + r ** 2)
        bore_cm3 = bore_mm3 / 1000.0
        stone_mm3 = (4.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * (stone_d / 2.0) ** 3
        free_mm3 = bore_mm3 - stone_mm3
        free_cm3 = free_mm3 / 1000.0
        Ro = od_bowl / 2.0; ro = od_mouth / 2.0
        outer_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * L * (Ro ** 2 + Ro * ro + ro ** 2)
        clay_cm3 = (outer_mm3 - bore_mm3) / 1000.0
        mass_g = clay_cm3 * rho
        d_end = d_bowl - (d_bowl - d_mouth) * bowl_len / L
        bowl_mm3 = (1.0 / 3.0) * math.pi * bowl_len * (R ** 2 + R * (d_end / 2.0) + (d_end / 2.0) ** 2)
        bowl_cm3 = bowl_mm3 / 1000.0
        capacity_g = bowl_cm3 * pack
        return {"bore_volume_mm3": round(bore_mm3, 2), "bore_volume_cm3": round(bore_cm3, 2), "stone_volume_mm3": round(stone_mm3, 2), "free_volume_cm3": round(free_cm3, 2), "clay_volume_cm3": round(clay_cm3, 2), "clay_mass_g": round(mass_g, 2), "bowl_volume_cm3": round(bowl_cm3, 2), "herb_capacity_g": round(capacity_g, 2)}

    def run(self):
        """Compute twice, print named results and SHA-256 digests."""
        a = self.compute()
        b = self.compute()
        sa = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(a.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        sb = hashlib.sha256(repr(sorted(b.items())).encode()).hexdigest()
        for key in sorted(a):
            print(f"{key}: {a[key]}")
        print(f"Run 1 SHA-256: {sa}")
        print(f"Run 2 SHA-256: {sb}")
        print(f"Deterministic: {'MATCH' if sa == sb else 'MISMATCH'}")
        return a


if __name__ == "__main__":
    SupplyCalculator().run()

use_program: To use the chillum, set the chillum stone inside first, then pack the bowl end by pressing it gently into ground herb and turning it a quarter turn each way, until the bowl section is full but not compressed. Hold the chillum at a slight angle, bring the flame just over the edge of the bowl, and start a slow draw, then tap out the ash when the bowl is spent. With no carb, there is nothing to clear: the smoke stops when the herb is gone. The traditional method cups both hands around the mouthpiece to form a chamber where smoke can collect and cool, and a damp safi cloth around the mouthpiece filters the smallest debris. The program in this record computes what the chillum holds and how it draws: the bore volume from the frustum formula, the free volume after the chillum stone, the glass volume and mass from the outer frustum, and the bowl-section capacity from the taper at the wide end. Run the demo to see the numbers, then change one input at a time — a longer tube, a wider bowl end, a bigger stone — and watch the capacity and the free volume move. The program is the use check: if the bowl capacity it reports is far above two grams for a pipe this size, the taper in the record is wrong, and the reader should re-measure the chillum before trusting it.
